description.en: The 3 leg chaturanga pose (Eka Pada Chaturanga Dandasana) is an advanced yoga pose that combines a low push up hold with a single leg raise. The lifter holds a chaturanga position with one leg lifted off the floor. It is a brutal upper body and core hold.

en: Begin in a high plank position.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Bend the elbows to lower the body to a low push up.
Stop with the elbows at 90 degrees and upper arms parallel.
Brace your core and keep the body steady.
Lift one leg off the floor extending it straight back.
Hold the three leg chaturanga position with steady breath.
Lower the leg. Switch legs and repeat.
Strong yoga upper body builder
Trains the chaturanga hold
Builds shoulder stability
No equipment needed
Strong core challenge
Builds the triceps

description.en: The assisted motion Russian twist uses a cable to add assistance and load to a Russian twist. The lifter sits and rotates side to side while the cable provides resistance. It is a useful oblique builder with constant tension.

en: Sit on the floor with the knees bent and feet flat.
Hold a cable handle with both hands at the chest.
Lean back to a comfortable angle.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Twist the torso to one side against the cable.
Pause briefly at the rotated position.
Twist back to the other side.
Continue alternating sides.
Loads the obliques
Constant cable tension
Strong twist variation
Builds the core
Useful oblique builder

description.en: The band overhead single arm triceps extension is a unilateral overhead tricep move that uses a resistance band. The lifter anchors the band underfoot and extends one arm overhead. It builds the long head of the triceps with portable resistance.

en: Anchor a resistance band under one foot.
Grip the band handle with one hand.
Bring the hand up so the elbow is by the ear.
Brace your core and keep the back straight.
Extend the arm fully overhead.
Squeeze the tricep hard at the top.
Lower the hand behind the head with control.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Trains the triceps
Strong band variation
Builds the long head
Useful for travel
Trains each side
Builds the upper arms

description.en: The band seated hip internal rotation is a seated hip rotator drill done with a band anchored to the side. The mover rotates the foot inward against band tension. It builds hip stability and internal rotation strength.

en: Sit on a bench with one foot flat on the floor.
Anchor a resistance band to the inside of the working foot.
Loop the band around the foot.
Sit tall with the chest up and back straight.
Brace your core and keep the knee in line.
Rotate the foot inward against the band tension.
Hold briefly at the rotated position.
Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Trains hip internal rotation
Builds hip stability
Strong rotator drill
Useful warm-up
Builds the glutes

description.en: The bar bicep curl performs an inverted row with a supinated (underhand) grip at a low bar height, focusing on curling the body toward the bar with bicep emphasis. The underhand grip and curl-focused technique shifts more demand to the biceps than a standard inverted row.

en: Set a bar at about hip height. Lie underneath with a supinated (underhand) grip.
Hang with arms extended, body straight.
Curl your body toward the bar by focusing on bending at the elbows — like a bicep curl.
Pull until your chin clears the bar.
Lower under control.
Focus on squeezing the biceps during the pull.
Adjust body angle for difficulty.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Bodyweight bicep exercise
Supinated grip maximizes bicep emphasis
Adjustable difficulty by body angle
No weights needed
Builds bicep pulling strength
Useful when no dumbbells are available

description.en: The barbell good morning is a hip-hinge exercise performed with a loaded barbell racked across the upper back. You hinge at the hips while keeping the back flat, then return to standing. The exercise builds the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back, and reinforces the hip-hinge pattern foundational to the deadlift. It demands strict form — start light and prioritize technique.

en: Set the barbell in a power rack at upper-chest height. Step under the bar and rack it across your upper back, in the same position as a low-bar back squat.
Unrack the bar with a slight knee bend, take two to three small steps back, and set your feet hip-width apart.
Soft-bend your knees and lock that knee angle for the entire lift. The knees should not change angle as you hinge.
Brace your core hard, lift your chest, and pull your shoulders back. Take a deep breath.
Hinge forward at the hips by pushing your butt back. Let your torso angle forward while keeping the bar in solid contact with your back and your back flat.
Lower until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor or until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings — whichever comes first. Do not round the lower back.
Drive your hips forward to stand back up, contracting your glutes and hamstrings. Lock out tall.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use much lighter weights than you would for squats — this lift is harder than it looks.
Builds the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back through a strong hip-hinge pattern
Reinforces the hinge mechanics foundational to the deadlift
Excellent accessory for strengthening a weak lower back in squats and deadlifts
Improves hamstring flexibility through loaded stretching
Builds a stronger back arch and torso position under load
Carries over to athletic movements requiring hip extension power

description.en: The barbell hang power clean is an Olympic lifting derivative where you start with the barbell at mid-thigh (hang position) and explosively pull it to the front rack. The "power" designation means you catch it in a partial squat rather than a full squat. It builds explosive hip drive, trap strength, and catching mechanics.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold the barbell with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Hinge at the hips to lower the bar to mid-thigh level (the hang position). Knees slightly bent.
Brace your core. Flat back. Shoulders over the bar.
Explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles — driving the bar upward.
Shrug your shoulders hard as the bar rises.
Pull yourself under the bar and catch it on your front shoulders (front rack) in a quarter-squat.
Stand up from the quarter-squat with the bar in the front rack.
Lower the bar back to the hang position and repeat.
Builds explosive hip drive and power
Develops trap strength and upward pull
Easier to learn than full cleans from the floor
Excellent athletic power exercise
Carries over to sport performance
Develops rate of force development

description.en: The barbell hang snatch starts from the hang position (bar held at mid-thigh) rather than the floor. This eliminates the first pull from the floor and emphasizes the explosive second pull and turnover. It is excellent for developing the power phase of the snatch and is more accessible than the full snatch from the floor.

en: Stand holding a barbell with a wide snatch grip. Let the bar hang at arm’s length at mid-thigh.
Set up: chest up, shoulders back, brace your core. Slight knee bend.
Begin by hinging slightly at the hips while keeping the bar against your thighs. The bar should travel down the legs to just above the knees.
From there, explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles (triple extension).
As the bar passes your hips, shrug aggressively and high-pull.
Pull yourself under the bar by dropping into a quarter squat.
Catch the bar overhead with arms locked out.
Stand fully to complete the lift. Use light weight while learning.
Trains the explosive second pull
More accessible than the full snatch
Builds total-body power
Develops triple extension
Excellent Olympic lift variation
Useful technique developer

description.en: The barbell step-up holds a barbell across the upper back and steps onto a box or bench. The barbell allows much heavier loading than dumbbells. Each rep builds single-leg strength on the stepping leg.

en: Set a barbell at upper-back height. Step under and place it across your upper traps.
Stand in front of a box or bench (knee height or just below).
Place your right foot on the box.
Drive through your right foot to step up onto the box. Bring your left foot up.
Stand fully on the box. Squeeze your right glute.
Step down with your left foot leading.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Use moderate to heavy weight. Aim for 8 to 10 reps per leg.
Heavy single-leg loading with barbell
Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally
Exposes left-right imbalances
Easier on knees than lunges for many lifters
Easy to load progressively
Carries over to athletic stepping power

description.en: The battling ropes Russian twist is a battle rope drill that uses a Russian twist pattern. The lifter holds both ropes and twists them side to side. It loads the obliques while training the shoulders and core.

en: Grip both battle rope ends with the hands together.
Stand with the feet shoulder width apart facing the anchor.
Lift the rope ends to chest height.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Twist the torso to one side and slam the ropes down.
Reverse the twist to the other side.
Slam the ropes down on each twist.
Continue alternating sides.
Loads the obliques
Burns calories
Strong rotational drill
Builds the shoulders
Useful for athletes

description.en: The cable deadlift performs a hip-hinge deadlift pattern using a low cable pulley instead of a barbell. The cable provides constant tension throughout — including at the top where a barbell deadlift loses tension. It is useful for hypertrophy and for teaching the hinge pattern.

en: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar or rope handle.
Face the cable. Grip the handle. Step back until the cable is taut.
Stand with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core.
Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt back. Let the cable pull the handle forward.
Lower until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings. Back flat.
Drive your hips forward to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Constant cable tension at the top — unlike a barbell.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Constant cable tension including at the top
Teaches the hip hinge pattern
Builds glutes and hamstrings
Easy to load progressively
Less spinal loading than barbell deadlifts
Useful for hypertrophy focus

description.en: The cable kneeling pull-through is a glute isolation exercise performed in a tall kneeling position facing away from a low cable. You hinge at the hips and pull the cable through between your legs by driving your hips forward. The kneeling position removes the quads, isolating the glutes and hamstrings.

en: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a rope handle.
Kneel facing away from the cable. Pass the rope between your legs from behind.
Grip both ends. Kneel tall. The cable should be taut.
Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back. Let the cable pull your hands back between your legs.
Drive your hips forward by squeezing your glutes.
Return to tall kneeling with hips fully extended.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Isolates the glutes without quad involvement
Kneeling removes leg drive
Constant cable tension throughout
Teaches proper hip hinge mechanics
Easy to load progressively
Excellent glute activation exercise

description.en: The cable overhead curl is a unique bicep isolation exercise where you stand between two high cable pulleys with both arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height (T position), then curl the handles toward your head. The arms-overhead position places the biceps in their most stretched position with constant cable tension.

en: Set two cable pulleys to high positions (above head height). Attach D-handles to each.
Stand between the cables. Grip both handles with arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height (T position), palms facing up.
Stand tall. Brace your core. Keep your upper arms parallel to the floor.
Curl both handles toward your head by bending at the elbows. Keep your upper arms still.
Continue until your forearms are vertical (or the handles approach your ears).
Squeeze your biceps hard at the top — focus on the peak contraction.
Slowly extend your arms back to the start over two seconds.
Maintain cable tension throughout. Use moderate weight.
Targets the biceps in their most stretched position
Constant cable tension throughout
Excellent for bicep peak development
Strict isolation — no body english possible
Easy to load progressively
Builds the bicep peak

description.en: The cable seated horizontal shrug uses a chest-height cable to train the middle trapezius and rhomboids through horizontal shoulder retraction. Pulling the shoulder blades back without bending the elbows isolates the scapular retractors. It is a strong choice for posture work and upper back development.

en: Sit at a cable row station with a single bar or rope attachment at chest height.
Grip the attachment with both hands and arms extended forward.
Sit tall with chest up and feet braced.
Brace your core.
Without bending your elbows, retract your shoulder blades back and together.
Allow the attachment to pull back slightly with the scapular movement.
Squeeze your middle traps and rhomboids hard at the back position.
Slowly extend your shoulder blades forward to the starting position.
Strict scapular retractor isolation
Builds middle traps and rhomboids
Improves posture
Useful for shoulder health
No elbow bending isolates the shrug
Strong functional movement for posture

description.en: The cable twisting standing row combines a single-arm cable row with a torso rotation. You stand sideways to the cable, pull the handle toward your hip, and rotate your torso. It builds back strength and rotational core power simultaneously.

en: Set a cable pulley to mid-chest height. Attach a D-handle.
Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your far hand.
Start with arm extended toward the cable, torso rotated toward the cable.
Row the handle toward your hip while simultaneously rotating your torso away from the cable.
Squeeze your lat and oblique at the end position.
Slowly return to start — extending arm and rotating back toward the cable.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Combines rowing with rotational core work
Builds back and oblique strength together
Constant cable tension
Functional pulling and rotation pattern
Easy to load progressively
Useful for sport-specific conditioning

description.en: The dumbbell Arnold press II is a seated variation of the classic Arnold press. Performed on a bench with a back support, it eliminates lower body involvement and lets you focus heavier loads on the shoulders. The wrist rotation through the press hits all three deltoid heads.

en: Sit on a bench with a vertical back support.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height with palms facing you.
Start with elbows tucked together in front of your face.
Press the dumbbells up while rotating your wrists outward.
At the top, palms face forward and arms are fully extended overhead.
Squeeze your shoulders at the lockout.
Lower the dumbbells back down while reversing the rotation.
Return to the starting position with palms facing you.
Seated version allows heavier loading
Hits all three deltoid heads through rotation
Back support eliminates lower body involvement
Builds shoulder size and definition
Smooth rotation creates time under tension
Excellent for hypertrophy training

description.en: The dumbbell close grip shoulder press sit up is a combo movement that combines a weighted sit up with a close-grip shoulder press. After sitting up with dumbbells held at the chest, you press the dumbbells overhead at the top of the sit up. The combination trains the abs and shoulders together with progressive load.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your chest with palms facing each other.
Brace your abs hard.
Sit up by curling your torso up.
Continue until your torso is upright.
At the top of the sit up, press both dumbbells overhead with arms extended.
Lower the dumbbells back to the chest.
Lower yourself back down to the floor with control.
Combines ab and shoulder work
Time-efficient combo movement
Builds total core strength
Strong tricep involvement
Useful for full body conditioning
Different stimulus than isolated lifts

description.en: The dumbbell incline fly on exercise ball is performed with the upper back resting on a stability ball and the body angled upward like an incline bench. The unstable surface forces the core and stabilizers to work hard while the dumbbells fly out and back to hit the upper chest. It builds chest detail and trunk control.

en: Sit on a stability ball holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Walk your feet forward and let the upper back roll onto the ball.
Press your hips up so your body forms an incline angle.
Press the dumbbells up over your chest with palms facing each other.
Open your arms out wide with a slight bend in the elbows.
Lower the dumbbells until you feel a stretch across the chest.
Squeeze the chest to bring the dumbbells back together over your chest.
Keep your hips up and core tight throughout.
Targets the upper chest
Builds core stability
Recruits stabilizer muscles
Improves balance
No bench needed
Versatile and travel-friendly

description.en: The dumbbell low windmill holds a dumbbell down at the hip on one side while you bend at the hips and reach the opposite hand toward the floor or your foot. Unlike the overhead windmill, the low version focuses on hip and oblique mobility without the overhead pressing demand. It is a strong hip mobility and core drill.

en: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out at about 45 degrees.
Hold a dumbbell in your right hand at hip level with arm extended down.
Place your left hand on your hip or extended out for balance.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Push your hips back to your right side as you bend forward and to the left.
Reach your left hand down toward your left foot or the floor.
Keep your right arm and the dumbbell hanging straight down toward your right leg.
Reverse the motion to stand back to the starting position. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Builds hip mobility and oblique strength
Trains anti-rotation core control
Stretches hamstrings and adductors
No overhead pressing demand
Strong functional movement pattern
Useful as a warm-up or accessory

description.en: The dumbbell rear delt row is a bent-over row performed with wide, flared elbows to shift emphasis from the lats to the rear deltoids and mid-traps. The key is keeping your elbows pointing out to the sides at shoulder height during the row.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand. Hinge forward at the hips.
Let the dumbbells hang below your chest.
Row with elbows flared wide — drive your elbows out to the sides at shoulder height.
Squeeze your rear delts and shoulder blades at the top.
Lower under control.
The wide elbows are the key cue — they shift work from lats to rear delts.
Use lighter weight than standard rows.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Targets rear delts over lats
Wide elbows shift the emphasis effectively
Builds shoulder balance
Simple form adjustment from standard rows
Easy to load progressively
Useful for posture improvement

description.en: The dumbbell renegade row to squat combines two compound movements into a flowing combo. From a renegade row position, you row each dumbbell, then jump or step your feet forward into a squat with the dumbbells at your shoulders. The combo trains back, legs, core, and conditioning together.

en: Place two dumbbells on the floor and assume a high plank position gripping them.
Set your feet wider than your hips for stability.
Row the right dumbbell up to your hip while bracing the core.
Lower the dumbbell, then row the left dumbbell up to your hip.
Lower the dumbbell back down.
Jump or step your feet forward toward your hands to enter a squat position.
Stand up with the dumbbells at your shoulders.
Lower back into the squat, then step or jump back to the starting plank position.
Trains back, legs, and core together
Strong conditioning element
Builds anti-rotation core strength
Time-efficient compound combo
Functional movement transitions
Excellent finisher for total body sessions

description.en: The dumbbell seated bicep curl is a bicep curl performed seated on a bench with a dumbbell in each hand. The seated position eliminates leg drive and torso swing, forcing stricter form and greater bicep isolation than the standing version. It is an excellent variation for lifters who tend to cheat on standing curls.

en: Sit on the end of a flat bench or on a bench with upright back support, feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing your body. Sit upright with chest tall.
Pull your shoulders back. Pin your elbows against your sides.
Curl both dumbbells up by bending at the elbows. Rotate your wrists outward as you curl so your palms face your shoulders at the top.
Continue until the dumbbells reach shoulder height. Squeeze your biceps hard for one second.
Lower the dumbbells under control over two seconds, rotating your wrists back to neutral.
Fully extend your arms at the bottom. Keep your torso completely upright throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. The seated position makes any cheating immediately obvious.
Eliminates leg drive and torso swing for strict form
Greater bicep isolation than standing curls
Independent dumbbells expose left-right imbalances
Makes cheating on reps immediately obvious
Allows full supination for peak contraction
Works at home with one pair of dumbbells and a bench

description.en: The dumbbell seated one leg calf raise palm up is a unilateral seated calf raise with the dumbbell held supinated. The bent knee position shifts the load to the soleus while the single leg setup exposes side to side weakness.

en: Sit on a bench with one foot flat on the floor.
Set the ball of that foot on a sturdy block or plate.
Hold a dumbbell vertically on the working thigh with a palm up grip.
Allow the heel to drop down for a deep calf stretch.
Brace the core and keep the torso upright.
Press up onto the toes by raising the heel as high as possible.
Squeeze the calf hard at the top.
Lower with control and repeat for all reps then switch.
Isolates the soleus one side at a time.
Bent knee shifts load to the deeper calf.
Palm up grip stabilizes the dumbbell on the thigh.
Builds calf size and ankle strength.
Useful for fixing calf imbalances.

description.en: The dumbbell side lunge with shoulder press combines two movements into one combo. As you step into a lateral lunge, you press the dumbbells overhead. The combo trains the legs through the side lunge and the shoulders through the press, with strong hip mobility demand and full body coordination.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level.
Position the dumbbells with palms facing forward.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Step laterally to the right with your right foot.
As you land, drop into a side lunge by sitting back on your right leg.
At the bottom of the lunge, press both dumbbells overhead.
Lock out the press at the bottom of the lunge.
Lower the dumbbells back to shoulder level as you push off your right foot to return to standing. Alternate sides.
Trains legs and shoulders in one combo
Builds hip mobility and adductor flexibility
Strong cardiovascular component
Time-efficient compound movement
Develops coordination across patterns
Functional carryover to athletic movement

description.en: The dumbbell superman is a loaded version of the superman exercise where you lie face down with arms extended overhead holding light dumbbells, then lift your arms, chest, and legs off the floor simultaneously. The added weight in the hands progressively overloads the upper-back and erector spinae.

en: Lie face down on the floor with legs extended back. Hold a light dumbbell in each hand with arms extended overhead, like superman.
Brace your core. Squeeze your glutes.
Simultaneously lift your arms, chest, and legs off the floor — like superman flying.
Lift the dumbbells as high as comfortable above the floor.
Hold for 1 to 2 seconds at the top. Squeeze your back and glutes.
Lower under control back to the floor. Stop just before touching down to maintain tension.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Use very light dumbbells (2 to 5 lbs) — the lever arm makes this much harder than it looks.
Adds progressive overload to superman holds
Builds upper back and glute strength
Develops shoulder mobility
Useful posture corrective exercise
Easy to scale by dumbbell weight
No bench needed

description.en: The external shoulder rotation stretch is a doorway-based stretch where you bend your elbow at 90 degrees and place your forearm against a doorframe with the elbow at shoulder height. Stepping forward stretches the front of the shoulder and pectoralis major. It is one of the simplest and most effective stretches for tight front shoulders.

en: Stand in a doorway. Bend your right elbow to 90 degrees.
Place your right forearm against the doorframe with the elbow at shoulder height.
Gently step your right foot forward through the doorway.
Feel the stretch through the front of your right shoulder and chest.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Adjust the elbow height to target different fibers — higher elbow stretches lower chest, lower elbow stretches upper chest.
Switch arms and repeat.
Avoid overstretching — go only to a comfortable depth.
Opens the front of the shoulder and chest
Improves shoulder external rotation range
Counteracts tight front delts from pressing
Easy to do in any doorway
No equipment needed
Quick and accessible

description.en: The EZ bar standing overhead press is a vertical pressing exercise performed standing with an EZ curl bar. The angled grip is more comfortable on the wrists than a straight barbell, and the standing position trains core stability. It is a useful overhead pressing variation for lifters with wrist issues.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip an EZ bar on the inner or outer angled portions with an overhand grip.
Hold the bar at upper-chest level. Brace your core hard.
Press the bar straight overhead by extending at the shoulders and elbows.
Move your head back slightly as the bar passes your face, then bring it back forward at lockout.
Lock out with the bar directly above your shoulders. Squeeze your glutes for stability.
Lower the bar under control to upper-chest level.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Use lighter weight than barbell pressing — the EZ grip changes the leverage.
Angled grip is easier on the wrists than a straight barbell
Standing position trains core stability
Useful overhead press variation for wrist issues
Builds the shoulders and triceps
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell pressing
Easy to set up

description.en: The floor T raise is a prone rear delt and upper back exercise performed face down on the floor. The arms raise out to the sides in a T shape and lift up off the floor. It strengthens the rear delts, rhomboids, and lower traps and is a staple of postural correction work.

en: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended out to the sides.
Position your arms in a T shape at shoulder height.
Place your hands palm-down on the floor.
Brace your core and keep your forehead resting on the floor.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Raise both arms straight up off the floor.
Lift as high as you can with full retraction.
Lower the arms slowly back to the floor.
Strengthens the rear delts
Builds the rhomboids and lower traps
Improves posture
No equipment required
Useful for desk workers
Bodyweight rear delt work

description.en: The front hamstring stretch is a standing single-leg hamstring stretch where you place your front leg straight in front with the heel down and toes lifted, then hinge forward at the hips over the front leg. It deeply stretches the hamstring of the front leg with no equipment needed.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Step your right foot forward about a foot. Keep the right leg straight and the right heel pressed into the floor.
Lift the toes of your right foot off the floor (dorsiflexion).
Bend your back (left) knee slightly. Place both hands on your left thigh for support.
Hinge forward at the hips over your right leg, keeping your back flat.
Continue hinging until you feel a deep stretch in your right hamstring.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Switch sides and repeat.
Deeply stretches the hamstring of the front leg
Targets one hamstring at a time
Easy to perform anywhere
No equipment needed
Improves hamstring flexibility for hinging exercises
Reveals left-right tightness

description.en: The hangboard half crimp is a finger and grip strength builder used by rock climbers. The lifter hangs from a hangboard edge with the fingers bent at the second knuckle in a half crimp position. The hold builds finger tendon strength and climbing grip.

en: Stand below a hangboard mounted overhead.
Reach up and grip an edge with your fingertips.
Set your fingers in a half crimp with the second knuckles bent.
Engage your shoulders and pull them down away from the ears.
Lift your feet off the ground to hang from the edge.
Hold the half crimp position with the body steady.
Keep the core braced and avoid swinging.
Lower your feet back down with control.
Builds climbing grip strength
Trains finger tendons
Useful for rock climbers
Strong forearm builder
Develops crushing grip
Climbing-specific carryover

description.en: The hanging straight twisting leg hip raise is an advanced ab move done from a dead hang. Lifting the legs straight up with a twist forces the obliques and lower abs to work hard while keeping the body controlled.

en: Hang from a pull-up bar with a shoulder width grip.
Allow the body to hang in a straight line.
Brace the core and keep the legs together.
Lift the straight legs up and across to one side.
Continue lifting until the toes pass the opposite hip.
Squeeze the obliques hard at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Alternate sides each rep or work one side at a time.
Hammers the lower abs and obliques.
Builds advanced core strength.
Trains grip endurance.
Improves shoulder stability.
Brutal core finisher.

description.en: The high knee step-up is a cardio-focused step-up variation where you drive the back knee up explosively after stepping onto the box. It combines lower-body strength with explosive hip flexion and cardiovascular conditioning. It is a popular HIIT exercise.

en: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench (knee-height).
Step your right foot up onto the box.
Drive through your right foot to push your body up explosively. As you reach standing, drive your left knee up to hip height (or higher).
Briefly hold the high-knee position on top of the box.
Lower your left foot back to the floor.
Step your right foot back down.
Repeat all reps on the right, then switch.
Move with explosive intent, not slow control.
Combines step-up strength with explosive cardio
Builds quad and glute power
Trains explosive hip flexion
Excellent HIIT exercise
No equipment needed beyond a box
Easy to scale with box height

description.en: The incline push-up is a regression of the standard push-up where you place your hands on an elevated surface (bench, box, or wall) instead of the floor. The higher your hands, the easier the lift. It is the best progression step between kneeling push-ups and full push-ups, and a useful warm-up for experienced lifters.

en: Place your hands on a sturdy elevated surface (bench, box, or counter) slightly wider than shoulder-width, fingers pointing forward.
Step your feet back so your body forms a straight line from heels to head.
Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders down and back. Keep your hips level.
Lower your chest toward the surface by bending at the elbows. Tuck your elbows at roughly 45 degrees from your torso.
Lower until your chest lightly touches or comes within an inch of the surface.
Press back up by extending at the elbows, driving your hands into the surface.
Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. Maintain the straight body line throughout.
Progress to a lower surface as you get stronger. Eventually transition to floor push-ups.
Effective progression step toward full push-ups
Easily scalable by changing surface height
Builds the chest, triceps, and shoulders with reduced load
Trains core stability through the plank position
No equipment needed beyond a sturdy surface
Excellent warm-up for experienced lifters

description.en: The inverse leg curl with bench pads is a nordic curl variation using a bench for foot support. The lifter kneels on the floor with the feet under the bench pads, then lowers the body forward. The hamstrings catch the body in an eccentric pattern.

en: Kneel on a pad behind a flat bench.
Hook the feet under the lower edge of the bench pads.
Set the shins flat on the floor with the feet locked.
Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line.
Lower the body forward by extending the knees.
Control the descent using the hamstrings.
At the bottom catch with the hands on the floor.
Push up with the arms and pull with the hamstrings to return.
Brutal hamstring builder
Trains eccentric strength
Builds posterior chain
No machine needed
Useful hamstring builder
Strong bench move

description.en: The inverted row II is a variation of the classic inverted row, performed underneath a low bar set in a power rack or Smith machine. Hanging horizontally from the bar with feet planted, you pull your chest up to the bar. The bodyweight load makes it accessible while still building real back strength.

en: Set a barbell in a power rack at about waist height.
Lie on the floor underneath the bar.
Grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, palms facing away.
Position your body in a straight line with heels on the floor.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Pull your chest up to the bar by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower yourself back down with control to a full hang.
Builds back strength with bodyweight
Accessible to lifters who cannot do pull-ups
Strong rhomboid and lat engagement
No weights required
Strong core engagement to maintain plank
Easy to scale by adjusting bar height

description.en: The kettlebell assisted Bulgarian split squat uses a wall, post, or sturdy support for the free hand during a single-arm Bulgarian split squat with a kettlebell. The hand support reduces balance demands, allowing beginners to focus on the strength pattern. It builds single-leg strength.

en: Position a bench or box behind your standing position.
Stand near a stable wall, post, or rack for hand support.
Hold a kettlebell in your right hand and place your left hand on the support.
Place the top of your left foot on the bench behind you.
Stand tall with most of your weight on the front leg.
Brace your core and lower into a split squat by bending the front knee.
Use the support hand for light balance assistance as needed.
Drive through the front foot to stand back to the starting position. Switch sides.
Beginner-friendly Bulgarian split squat
Reduces balance demands
Allows focus on the strength pattern
Stepping stone to free-standing version
Builds single-leg strength
Useful for rehab or movement re-education

description.en: The kettlebell half kneeling one arm bottoms up press is a serious shoulder stability and grip drill. The bottoms up grip with the bell inverted demands intense forearm activation while pressing from a half kneeling position.

en: Drop into a half kneeling stance with one knee on the floor.
Hold a kettlebell upside down at the rack position with the bell above the wrist.
Squeeze the handle hard to keep the bell balanced overhead.
Brace the core and keep the torso tall.
Press the kettlebell straight up to lockout overhead.
Keep the wrist neutral and the bell perfectly vertical.
Lower the kettlebell back to the rack with full control.
Complete all reps on one side then switch.
Builds elite shoulder stability and grip strength.
Half kneeling stance kills momentum and isolates the shoulder.
Trains the core to resist tipping under load.
Sharpens overhead pressing precision.
Improves the rotator cuff and shoulder health.
Develops mental focus through the unstable bell.

description.en: The kettlebell wrist curl targets the wrist flexors by sitting on a bench, resting your forearm on your thigh, and curling the KB up by flexing at the wrist. The KB handle position provides a unique grip challenge compared to dumbbells.

en: Sit on a bench. Hold a light KB in your right hand.
Rest your right forearm on your right thigh, wrist hanging off the knee.
Let the KB hang with your wrist extended (hand hanging down).
Curl the KB up by flexing your wrist.
Squeeze your forearm flexors at the top.
Lower under control.
Complete reps, then switch.
Use light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Builds forearm flexor strength
KB handle provides a unique grip challenge
Easy to load progressively
Useful for grip-intensive activities
Simple setup
Builds wrist health

musclesWorked: Wrist flexors (flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris)

description.en: The knee circles stretch is a gentle warm-up move performed by standing with knees together and slightly bent, hands on the knees, and drawing slow circles with both knees together. It loosens up the knee joints, hips, and ankles before training. It is a staple of athletic warm-ups and physical therapy routines.

en: Stand with your feet together and knees slightly bent.
Place both hands on your knees.
Lean forward slightly so your weight is on your hands.
Brace your core for stability.
Slowly draw circles with both knees together.
Move in one direction for a comfortable number of reps.
Reverse and circle in the other direction.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
Warms up the knees and hips
Improves joint mobility
Useful before lower body training
Loosens stiff knees
Gentle on the body

description.en: The kneeling iliopsoas stretch is a classic kneeling lunge stretch that targets the iliopsoas and hip flexors. It is one of the most effective ways to relieve tightness caused by long hours of sitting. Athletes and desk workers alike rely on it to keep the hips healthy.

en: Kneel on the floor with one knee down and the other foot in front.
Place a pad under the back knee for comfort.
Position the front foot directly under the front knee.
Tuck your pelvis slightly to lengthen the lower back.
Squeeze the back glute to deepen the stretch.
Press your hips gently forward until you feel a stretch in the front of the back hip.
Hold the position and breathe deeply.
Slowly come out of the stretch and switch sides.
Opens tight hip flexors
Relieves hip stiffness from sitting
Improves hip mobility
Useful for runners and lifters
Lengthens the iliopsoas and quads

description.en: The landmine floor one arm chest fly is a unilateral chest fly done with a landmine on the floor. The arcing path of the bar end and the floor stop create a fly motion that isolates the pec on the working side.

en: Lie on the floor next to a landmine setup.
Grab the end of the landmine bar with one hand.
Position the working arm out to the side with a slight elbow bend.
Brace the core and press the back flat to the floor.
Sweep the bar end across the body in an arc.
Stop when the working hand reaches the centerline of the chest.
Squeeze the pec hard at the top.
Lower with control to the start and repeat for all reps then switch.
Isolates one side of the chest.
Floor stops the range to protect the shoulder.
Trains anti-rotation core stability.
Useful chest accessory.
Builds the pectorals.

description.en: The landmine rear lunge is performed holding the end of a landmine bar at chest level while stepping back into a reverse lunge. The fixed arc of the landmine bar makes the movement more stable than free weights and easier on the wrists than a barbell front rack. The reverse lunge pattern emphasizes the glutes and quads.

en: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment or wedged in a corner.
Load the free end with weight plates.
Pick up the free end and bring it to chest level with both hands.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Step back with your right leg into a reverse lunge.
Lower until your back knee almost touches the floor.
Push through the front foot to drive back to standing. Alternate legs.
Loaded reverse lunge with stable bar path
Easier on wrists than barbell front rack
Builds glute and quad strength
Strong core engagement
Develops single leg stability
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The low glute bridge on floor is a small range glute bridge that keeps the hips low. The lifter only lifts the hips slightly off the floor for high tension on the glutes. It is useful for activation and high rep glute work.

en: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat.
Place the arms at the sides palms down.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lift the hips just slightly off the floor.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the small lift.
Lower with control nearly back to the floor.
Stop just before the hips touch and lift again.
Continue the small range pulses.
Builds the glutes
High tension activation
Strong glute drill
Useful warm-up
Builds glute endurance

description.en: The medicine ball lunge with biceps curl is a hybrid leg and arm move. The lifter holds a medicine ball at the hips and steps forward into a lunge while curling the ball up to the chest. The combo trains the legs and biceps in one rep.

en: Stand tall holding a medicine ball with both hands at the hips.
Brace your core and set the feet hip width.
Step forward with one leg into a long lunge.
Lower until the back knee nearly touches the floor.
At the same time curl the medicine ball up to the chest.
Squeeze the biceps at the top of the curl.
Push back through the front heel to standing while lowering the ball.
Alternate legs each rep.
Combo leg and arm move
Trains coordination
Builds full body strength
Strong functional pattern
Useful conditioning combo
Builds bicep size

description.en: The one legged upward bow pose eka pada urdhva dhanurasana is an advanced yoga backbend done from upward bow with one leg lifted. The single leg variation deeply stretches the chest, hip flexors, and quads while challenging shoulder and core stability.

en: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat.
Place the hands by the ears with fingers pointing toward the shoulders.
Press the hips up and lift into upward bow.
Press the chest open and straighten the arms.
Brace the core and squeeze the glutes.
Lift one leg straight up toward the ceiling.
Hold the pose with the leg lifted.
Lower with control then switch sides.
Stretches the chest deeply.
Opens the hip flexors.
Builds shoulder strength.
Trains balance.
Advanced backbend progression.

description.en: The power sled triceps extension is a sled drag variation focused on the triceps. The lifter grips the sled strap or rope behind the body and extends the elbows back to pull the sled forward. The pattern loads the triceps in their concentric pull.

en: Attach a strap or rope to a power sled.
Stand facing away from the sled and grip the strap behind.
Walk forward to take tension on the strap.
Set a slight forward lean and bend the elbows.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Extend the elbows back hard pulling the strap.
As the elbows lock out the sled drags forward.
Step forward to take new tension and continue the drags.
Strong tricep builder
Adds sled conditioning
Builds tricep size
Useful arm builder
Strong sled move
Builds posterior shoulder

description.en: The quadriceps lying stretch is a side-lying version of the standing quad stretch. Lying on your side eliminates balance demands and lets you focus on the stretch. The hand pulls the top heel back toward the glute, lengthening both the quadriceps and hip flexor.

en: Lie on your side with your bottom leg extended straight.
Bend the top knee and reach back to grab the top ankle.
Pull the top heel toward the same-side glute.
Keep your hips stacked and squared.
Push the top hip forward slightly to deepen the stretch.
Hold the position and breathe deeply.
Release the leg slowly.
Roll to the other side and repeat.
Stretches the quadriceps
Lengthens the hip flexors
No balance required
Easier than standing version
Useful for tight quads

description.en: The resistance band foot external rotation is an ankle strengthening drill done with a resistance band. The mover sits with the band anchored to the foot and rotates the foot outward. It builds the peroneals and ankle stability.

en: Sit on the floor with the legs extended.
Anchor a resistance band to the inside of the working foot.
Loop the band around the ball of the foot.
Brace your core and keep the back straight.
Rotate the foot outward against the band tension.
Hold briefly at the rotated position.
Return with control to the start.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Builds ankle stability
Trains the peroneals
Strong rehab drill
Useful for ankle health
Builds lower leg strength

description.en: The resistance band leg curl is a hamstring isolation exercise performed lying face down with a resistance band anchored in front of you and looped around your ankles. You curl your heels toward your glutes against the band tension, mimicking a lying leg curl machine.

en: Anchor a resistance band to a low point in front of you.
Lie face down on the floor with legs extended toward the anchor.
Loop the band around both ankles.
Move away from the anchor until the band is taut with legs extended.
Curl both heels toward your glutes by bending at the knees.
Squeeze your hamstrings at the top of the curl.
Slowly extend your legs back to the start under control.
Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Isolates the hamstrings at home
Mimics the lying leg curl machine
Constant band tension throughout
Highly portable
Useful for hamstring rehab or activation
Easy to scale by band thickness

description.en: The resistance band serratus wall slide with foam roll is an advanced scapular activation drill. Looping a band around the wrists while rolling a foam roller up a wall forces active engagement of the serratus to keep the band tense throughout the slide.

en: Loop a small resistance band around both wrists.
Stand facing a wall with a foam roller pressed against it.
Place both forearms on the roller with the band stretched.
Brace the core and press the arms forward into the roller.
Roll the foam roller up the wall while reaching overhead.
Keep the band taut throughout to engage the serratus.
Lower with control to the start.
Continue for the working set.
Activates the serratus anterior.
Band trains scapular control.
Improves overhead mobility.
Builds shoulder health.
Useful warm-up.

description.en: The rocking ankle stretch is a dynamic ankle mobility drill performed in a half-kneeling position. You rock the front knee forward over the toes repeatedly, mobilizing the ankle joint into dorsiflexion. It is essential for improving squat depth and any movement that requires good ankle mobility.

en: Kneel on your right knee with your left foot flat in front in a half-kneeling position.
Place both hands on your left knee or on the floor for stability.
Keep your left foot flat. Rock your left knee forward over your left toes.
Continue forward until you feel a stretch through your left ankle and lower calf.
Rock back to the starting position.
Continue rocking forward and back rhythmically for 10 to 15 reps.
Switch sides and repeat.
Make sure your heel stays planted throughout.
Improves ankle dorsiflexion mobility
Critical for squat depth
Helps prevent knee tracking issues
Excellent warm-up before lower-body training
No equipment needed
Quick and accessible

description.en: The side neck stretch is a simple stretch where you tilt your head sideways toward one shoulder, often using the hand to gently increase the stretch. It targets the upper trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles, providing quick relief from tension caused by sitting, screen time, and stress.

en: Sit or stand tall. Pull your shoulders back and down.
Tilt your head to the right, bringing your right ear toward your right shoulder.
Gently place your right hand on the left side of your head and use light pressure to deepen the stretch.
Keep your left shoulder pulled down and back — do not let it shrug up toward the stretching ear.
Feel the stretch through the left side of your neck and upper trap.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Release and switch sides.
Apply only gentle pressure with the hand — never force the neck stretch.
Relieves neck and trap tension
Quick and accessible — works anywhere
Counteracts the effects of screen time and stress
No equipment needed
Excellent stretch for desk workers
Improves head and neck posture

description.en: The sitting sumo left twist stretch combines a deep sumo squat with a left torso rotation. The position opens the hips, obliques, and chest in one stretch.

en: Stand with the feet wide and toes turned out.
Lower into a deep sumo squat keeping the chest tall.
Rest the elbows on the inside of the knees.
Brace the core and place the right hand on the floor in front.
Reach the left hand up toward the ceiling.
Rotate the torso to the left following the hand.
Open the chest and feel the stretch through the obliques.
Hold the stretch for the desired duration.
Opens the hips and adductors.
Stretches the obliques through rotation.
No equipment needed.
Improves squat depth.
Excellent warm up before lower body work.
Carryover to thoracic mobility.

description.en: Split jacks are a hybrid cardio exercise combining a split-stance jumping jack pattern. You alternate which foot is forward in a small split stance while raising and lowering your arms like a jumping jack. They build coordination, leg endurance, and cardiovascular conditioning with a unique movement pattern.

en: Stand tall with feet together, arms at your sides.
Jump and split your feet front-to-back into a short split stance — right foot forward, left foot back.
Simultaneously raise your arms out and up overhead like a jumping jack.
Jump and switch feet — left foot forward, right foot back.
Lower your arms back to your sides as you switch feet, then raise them again on the next switch.
Continue alternating front foot rapidly. Move at a brisk pace.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Land softly.
Perform for 30 to 60 seconds per set.
Combines coordination, cardio, and leg endurance
Builds quad and calf endurance
Develops timing and rhythm
No equipment needed
Engaging variation on standard jumping jacks
Excellent warm-up or HIIT exercise

description.en: The strongman shield carry is a loaded carry where you hold a heavy plate, shield, or flat implement at chest height (like a medieval shield) and walk for distance. The front-loaded position challenges the biceps, anterior delts, and anti-flexion core.

en: Stand tall. Hold a heavy weight plate flat against your chest with both hands.
Hug the plate close to your body. Arms bent, elbows in.
Brace your core hard. Pull shoulders back.
Walk forward with controlled strides.
Maintain upright posture — the weight pulls you forward.
Walk for the desired distance or time.
Set the plate down with control.
Use heavy weight for short distances.
Builds anti-flexion core strength
Develops bicep and shoulder endurance
Simple setup with a weight plate
Excellent full-body conditioning
Useful strongman training
Builds grip and hugging strength

description.en: The suspender close grip chest press is a TRX chest press with a narrow neutral grip. The lifter grips the handles together with palms facing in, then presses with the elbows tucked tight to the body. The narrow grip biases the triceps and inner chest.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip the handles with palms facing each other and hands close together.
Walk the feet back so the body leans forward at an angle.
Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line.
Lower the body by bending the elbows tight against the sides.
Stop with the chest near the handles.
Press back up to lockout extending the elbows.
Squeeze the chest and triceps at the top.
Strong tricep builder
Trains the inner chest
No bench needed
Useful chest move
Strong TRX move
Builds upper body size

description.en: The suspender forward lunge with rear fly pairs a TRX assisted forward lunge with a rear delt fly. The lifter steps into a lunge while pulling the handles wide for a fly. It builds legs, glutes, and rear delts in one combo move.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip the handles with both hands at chest height.
Stand facing the anchor with feet together.
Step one foot forward into a lunge.
Lower the back knee toward the floor.
At the bottom of the lunge pull the handles wide in a rear fly.
Push back to start while bringing the handles together.
Alternate legs each rep.
Combines legs and shoulders
Strong combo move
Builds the rear delts
Trains the quads
Useful functional move

description.en: The suspender self assisted chest dip is a TRX dip variation with a forward chest lean to bias the pectorals. The lifter dips between the handles with feet on the floor for assistance. It builds the lower chest and triceps.

en: Set the suspension trainer to elbow height.
Grip the handles with palms facing inward.
Lean forward at the hips to bias the chest.
Step the feet forward for assistance.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lower the body by bending the elbows.
Keep the chest leaning forward at the bottom.
Press back up to lockout.
Builds the chest
Trains the triceps
Strong dip variation
Useful for chest size
Adjustable assistance

description.en: The suspension trainer hip abduction is a TRX glute medius isolator. The lifter places one foot in a foot cradle and from a side plank position abducts the suspended leg out to the side. The TRX adds resistance and builds strong hip abductor strength.

en: Set the suspension trainer foot cradles low.
Place one foot in a cradle and lie on your side.
Set the bottom forearm on the floor under the shoulder.
Press up into a side plank with the body in a straight line.
Brace your core and squeeze the bottom glute.
Lift the suspended leg up away from the bottom leg.
Squeeze the glute medius hard at the top.
Lower the leg with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong glute medius isolator
Trains hip stability
Strong TRX glute move
Builds side-plank endurance
Useful for athletes
Strong hip abductor builder

description.en: Weighted hip thrusts add external load — a barbell, dumbbell, plate, or weighted vest — to the standard hip thrust to drive progressive overload of the glutes. Adding load is essential once bodyweight hip thrusts become easy. The weight is placed across the hips and supported with the hands.

en: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench. Place a barbell, dumbbell, or weight plate across your hips.
Use a barbell pad or folded towel to cushion the weight against your hip bones.
Plant your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Hold the weight with both hands to keep it steady.
Brace your core. Tuck your chin slightly.
Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips and the weight.
Continue until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Do not hyperextend the lower back.
Lower under control. Touch lightly, then drive up again.
Allows progressive overload of the glutes
Most effective glute mass builder
Easy to scale by changing weight
Targets the glutes without spinal compression of squats
Easier on the lower back than heavy squats and deadlifts
Builds glute strength that carries over to all lower-body lifts

description.en: The weighted incline svend press is performed lying on an incline bench, squeezing a weight plate between the palms in front of the chest. The plate presses forward and back while the hands squeeze hard. The incline angle biases the upper chest while the squeeze nails the inner pec.

en: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees.
Hold a weight plate between your palms in front of your chest.
Lie back on the bench with feet flat on the floor.
Squeeze your palms hard against the plate.
Brace your core and keep your back against the bench.
Press the plate straight up and forward away from your chest.
Maintain the squeeze through your hands the entire rep.
Lower the plate slowly back to your chest.
Hits the upper inner chest
Strong chest contraction
Constant squeeze tension
Useful as a finisher
No bar required
Joint-friendly chest move

description.en: Weighted lying neck flexion is a neck strengthening exercise where you lie face up on a bench with a weight plate on your forehead (cushioned with a towel) and curl your chin toward your chest. It builds the sternocleidomastoid and front neck muscles, important for contact sports and neck health.

en: Lie face up on a flat bench with your head hanging off the end.
Place a folded towel on your forehead. Place a light weight plate on the towel.
Hold the plate with both hands to keep it secure.
Start with your head tilted back (extended).
Curl your chin toward your chest by flexing your neck forward.
Squeeze the front of your neck at the top.
Lower under control back to the starting position.
Use very light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps. Protect your cervical spine.
Builds front neck strength
Important for contact sport athletes
Develops the sternocleidomastoid
Helps prevent neck injuries
Simple setup with a plate and towel
Easy to load progressively with small increments
